nodes.name: safeWriteFile
nodes.summary: Writes data to a file path, refusing to follow symlinks to prevent symlink-based write attacks.

nodes.name: safeJsonParse
nodes.summary: Parses a JSON string into a plain object, stripping prototype-pollution keys (__proto__, constructor, prototype) and returning a typed ok/error discriminated union.

nodes.name: oauth-proxy.ts
nodes.summary: Implements the GitLabOAuthServerProvider class which acts as an MCP OAuth proxy to GitLab, supporting passthrough mode, callback-proxy mode (where the MCP server intermediates the OAuth callback), and stateless mode for multi-pod deployments using sealed JWT-like tokens.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses a custom BoundedLRUMap for in-memory caching of pending auth transactions and client registrations with configurable max size and TTL-based expiry.

nodes.name: BoundedLRUMap
nodes.summary: A bounded LRU cache implemented on top of Map that evicts the least-recently-used entry when the max size is reached. Provides a getAndDelete method for one-time-use entries.

nodes.name: GitLabOAuthServerProvider
nodes.summary: Implements the MCP OAuthServerProvider interface for GitLab, handling DCR client registration, authorization redirects, PKCE-based token exchange, token refresh, token verification, callback proxy flow, and token revocation.

nodes.name: createGitLabOAuthProvider

nodes.name: oauth.ts
nodes.summary: Implements a standalone GitLab OAuth2 client with PKCE support that manages token storage on disk, starts a local HTTP callback server for the browser-based authorization flow, and coordinates multiple concurrent MCP instance authentications on a shared port.
nodes.languageNotes: Manages a process-level pendingAuthRequests Map to allow multiple MCP instances sharing the same callback port to each receive their own token without races.

nodes.name: GitLabOAuth
nodes.summary: Encapsulates the full GitLab OAuth2 PKCE flow including authorization URL generation, code exchange, token refresh, disk-based token persistence, and a shared local callback HTTP server for browser-initiated auth.

nodes.name: initializeOAuthClient
nodes.summary: Creates a GitLabOAuth client from environment variables and triggers the browser OAuth flow if no cached token exists, returning both the client instance and the initial access token.

nodes.name: initializeOAuth
nodes.summary: Convenience wrapper around initializeOAuthClient that returns only the access token string.

nodes.name: client-id.ts
nodes.summary: Implements signed (HMAC) client_id tokens for OAuth Dynamic Client Registration, embedding the DCR registration payload so any pod with the shared secret can reconstruct client metadata without shared storage.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses HMAC signing (not encryption) since the DCR payload (redirect URIs, grant types) is not confidential.

nodes.name: mintClientId
nodes.summary: Mints a signed client_id token embedding redirect URIs, grant types, and a random nonce so registrations remain distinct across calls.

nodes.name: openClientId
nodes.summary: Verifies a signed client_id token and returns the embedded payload, returning null on any verification failure.

nodes.name: looksLikeStatelessClientId
nodes.summary: Heuristically detects stateless client_ids by checking for the 'v1.cid.' prefix to distinguish them from legacy identifiers.

nodes.name: codec.ts
nodes.summary: Core wire-format codec for stateless tokens providing HMAC-signed and AES-256-GCM sealed token formats with rotation-aware multi-slot key verification.
nodes.languageNotes: Two distinct formats: signed (v1.<purpose>.<payload>.<hmac>) for non-confidential payloads, and sealed (v1.<purpose>.<nonce||ciphertext||tag>) for secret payloads using AES-256-GCM AEAD.

nodes.name: sign
nodes.summary: Mints a signed HMAC token from the current key slot, prefixing purpose tag to the HMAC input to prevent cross-purpose forgery.

nodes.name: verify
nodes.summary: Verifies a signed token against all available key slots (current + previous) with constant-time MAC comparison and TTL enforcement.

nodes.name: seal
nodes.summary: Encrypts a payload using AES-256-GCM with the purpose tag as AEAD associated data, producing a sealed token that cannot be repurposed.

nodes.name: open
nodes.summary: Decrypts a sealed AEAD token trying all available key slots, enforcing TTL and returning the decoded payload with the accepted slot.

nodes.name: errors.ts
nodes.summary: Defines typed error classes for the stateless token codec, including StatelessCodecError for token verification failures and StatelessConfigError for misconfiguration at startup.

nodes.name: StatelessCodecError
nodes.summary: Typed error carrying a reason code and purpose tag for token verification failures, enabling callers to translate to appropriate OAuth or HTTP errors.

nodes.name: StatelessConfigError
nodes.summary: Error thrown during module initialization when the OAUTH_STATELESS_SECRET environment variable is missing or invalid.

nodes.name: index.ts
nodes.summary: Public barrel module for the stateless token codec, re-exporting all types and functions from sub-modules as a stable API surface.

nodes.name: pending-auth.ts
nodes.summary: Implements AEAD-sealed OAuth state tokens for callback-proxy mode, carrying the PendingAuthTransaction (including the PKCE code_verifier secret) so any pod can process the callback without shared storage.

nodes.name: mintPendingAuthState
nodes.summary: Seals a PendingAuthPayload (client ID, redirect URI, PKCE verifier) into a URL-safe state parameter for the OAuth consent redirect.

nodes.name: openPendingAuthState
nodes.summary: Opens a sealed OAuth state parameter and validates required fields, returning null on any failure to prevent leaking error details.

nodes.name: secret.ts
nodes.summary: Keyring loader and HKDF-based subkey derivation for stateless mode, loading master secrets from environment variables and deriving per-purpose keys to achieve cryptographic domain separation.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses HKDF-SHA256 with a purpose tag as the info parameter, so each stateless purpose (client_id, session_id, etc.) gets a distinct derived key from the same master secret.

nodes.name: loadKeyMaterialFromEnv
nodes.summary: Loads current and optional previous master secrets from environment variables, enabling stateless mode with key rotation support.

nodes.name: deriveSubkeys
nodes.summary: Returns HKDF-derived subkeys for all available key slots (current + previous) for a given purpose, used by the codec for rotation-aware verification.

nodes.name: deriveSubkey

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: Start with the README to understand what @zereight/mcp-gitlab is: a comprehensive TypeScript-based GitLab MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that bridges AI clients like Claude, Cursor, and VS Code to the full GitLab API. It covers the three authentication modes (Personal Access Token, local OAuth2, and MCP OAuth proxy), the three transport modes (stdio for local use, SSE for legacy remote, Streamable HTTP for modern remote), and a tool registry spanning 170+ GitLab operations across 16 toolsets. Reading this first gives you the vocabulary — PAT, toolsets, stateless mode, dynamic API URL — that every subsequent file uses.

tour.title: Configuration & Environment
tour.description: Before any code runs, config.ts reads CLI arguments and environment variables to produce a single typed configuration object that every other module depends on. It resolves transport mode, authentication method, OAuth settings, stateless parameters, proxy settings, and the GitLab API base URL — essentially translating the user's `.env` file into strongly-typed TypeScript constants. The companion .env.example shows every variable that config.ts understands, making these two files the complete contract between the operator and the server.
tour.languageLesson: TypeScript's `as const` and union types let config.ts express transport mode as a discriminated union (stdio | sse | streamable-http), turning runtime string checks into compile-time exhaustiveness guarantees throughout the codebase.

tour.title: Server Entry Point
tour.description: index.ts is the monolithic heart of the server — 12,000+ lines — that reads the configuration from Step 2 and wires together every GitLab API tool handler, the three transport adapters, and the OAuth and stateless session middleware into a single running MCP server. Its sheer size reflects a deliberate architectural choice: all tool implementations live inline next to their schema declarations, making each GitLab operation self-contained and grep-friendly at the cost of file length. Following its startup sequence reveals the full request lifecycle: config load → transport binding → tool registration → request dispatch.

tour.title: Authentication Layer
tour.description: The server supports three auth paths, each implemented as a separate module. oauth.ts handles the local browser-based PKCE flow, spinning up an ephemeral HTTP callback server and storing tokens on disk. oauth-proxy.ts implements GitLabOAuthServerProvider — the MCP-level OAuth proxy that lets remote AI clients authenticate through the MCP server rather than directly to GitLab. auth-retry.ts provides a thin fetch wrapper used by all tool handlers: if GitLab returns 401, it silently refreshes the OAuth token via a mutex-coalesced refresh and replays the request, making auth failures transparent to the caller.
tour.languageLesson: Mutex coalescing in auth-retry.ts prevents a thundering-herd of concurrent 401s from each triggering their own refresh: the first refresh acquires a lock, subsequent 401s wait on the same promise, and all of them receive the single new token once it resolves.

tour.title: OAuth Setup Guide
tour.description: The docs/oauth-setup.md document complements the auth code from Step 4 by walking through all three OAuth modes from the operator's perspective: registering a GitLab application, choosing between local PKCE, MCP proxy, and remote header-based authorization. It also explains when to use each mode — local stdio deployments use the browser PKCE flow, while containerized or multi-tenant deployments need the MCP OAuth proxy or remote authorization headers. Reading this alongside oauth.ts and oauth-proxy.ts closes the loop between the implementation and its real-world deployment scenarios.

tour.title: Stateless Horizontal Scaling
tour.description: The stateless/ module solves a fundamental problem for Kubernetes deployments: how can multiple pod replicas share sessions without a shared database? The answer is to encode all session state — bearer tokens, OAuth PKCE verifiers, Mcp-Session-Id payloads — into cryptographically signed or sealed tokens using HMAC-SHA256 and AES-256-GCM. stateless/index.ts is the public barrel; stateless/secret.ts loads the OAUTH_STATELESS_SECRET and derives per-purpose subkeys via HKDF; stateless/codec.ts implements the wire-format sign/seal operations with multi-slot key rotation support. The higher-level modules (session-id.ts, pending-auth.ts, stored-tokens.ts, client-id.ts) each apply the codec to a specific OAuth state artifact.
tour.languageLesson: HKDF (HMAC-based Key Derivation Function) derives multiple independent subkeys from one master secret by mixing in a 'purpose' string as context. This means compromising the client_id signing key does not expose the session encryption key, even though both come from the same OAUTH_STATELESS_SECRET.

tour.title: Stateless Module Details
tour.description: The remaining stateless sub-modules handle each OAuth artifact that needs to cross pod boundaries. pending-auth.ts seals the PendingAuthTransaction (including the PKCE code_verifier) into the OAuth 'state' parameter so any pod can handle the callback; stored-tokens.ts seals the GitLab access/refresh token pair into a proxy authorization code for the token exchange step; client-id.ts embeds the Dynamic Client Registration payload into a signed client_id token so any pod can reconstruct client metadata without storage. stateless/errors.ts and stateless/types.ts provide the shared error classes and wire-format type definitions that all these modules depend on.
tour.languageLesson: AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data) provides both confidentiality and integrity in one operation. AES-256-GCM's authentication tag detects any tampering with the ciphertext before decryption, so a pod can safely reject tokens modified in transit without needing a separate HMAC check.

tour.title: Tool Registry & Schemas
tour.description: tools/registry.ts is the catalog that defines every MCP tool the server exposes: it declares TOOLSET_DEFINITIONS (the 16 groupings like 'mrs', 'issues', 'pipelines'), maps each tool name to its Zod schema, and provides the helper functions that index.ts calls at startup to filter the active toolset based on GITLAB_TOOLSETS and GITLAB_READ_ONLY_MODE environment variables. schemas.ts is the companion library of 170+ Zod schemas for every GitLab API request and response type — validated at the MCP protocol boundary before any HTTP call is made. customSchemas.ts adds reusable boolean coercion schemas that handle the string/number/boolean ambiguity common in HTTP query parameters.
tour.languageLesson: Zod schemas serve double duty here: they validate incoming MCP tool arguments at runtime AND generate the JSON Schema that the MCP SDK advertises to the AI client. utils/schema.ts's toJSONSchema wrapper strips redundant keys and fixes nullable field handling to reduce the token count in the tool manifest sent to the AI.

tour.title: Utility Layer
tour.description: The utils/ directory provides four focused helpers used throughout index.ts tool handlers. utils/url.ts normalizes any GitLab API base URL to end in /api/v4. utils/helpers.ts provides regex-based diff file filtering (for excluded_file_patterns), merge commit counting, and webhook event summarization. utils/patch-helper.ts implements the two content-patching strategies used by update_issue_description_patch: a search-and-replace block format and standard unified-diff application, each with dry-run preview support. utils/schema.ts exports toJSONSchema, wrapping zodToJsonSchema to produce lean tool descriptions that minimize token consumption in the MCP manifest.

tour.title: Connection Pool & Dynamic Routing
tour.description: gitlab-client-pool.ts enables a single MCP server deployment to route to multiple GitLab instances simultaneously. When ENABLE_DYNAMIC_API_URL is set, each tool invocation can carry an X-Gitlab-Api-Url header specifying a different GitLab host; the pool maintains a per-host Node.js http.Agent with keep-alive connections, respects NO_PROXY patterns for corporate proxy bypass, and enforces a maximum pool size. This is what makes the 'dynamic API URL' enterprise deployment pattern possible — one server process serving multiple teams pointing at different GitLab installations.

tour.title: OMG Workflow Sub-Server
tour.description: mcp-server/ is a separate, self-contained MCP server package for the OMG multi-agent workflow framework. Its entry point (mcp-server/src/index.ts) registers four tool groups: memory-tools.ts for persistent named memory across sessions, state-tools.ts for shared multi-agent workflow state, prd-tools.ts for structured Product Requirements Document CRUD, and model-router.ts for complexity-based Haiku/Sonnet/Opus routing. This sub-server runs independently of the main GitLab MCP server and is designed to be composed alongside it in a multi-server AI agent setup, providing the 'brain' state while the main server provides the GitLab 'hands'.

tour.title: Test Infrastructure
tour.description: The test/ directory is built around two reusable utilities: test/utils/mock-gitlab-server.ts is an Express-based fake GitLab API that every integration test spins up locally, providing token auth, in-memory state for issues and MRs, and configurable routes; test/utils/server-launcher.ts spawns the actual MCP server process and discovers its port for health checks. The test/clients/ directory provides MCPClientInterface abstractions for all three transports, so any test can swap between stdio, SSE, and Streamable HTTP without changing test logic. test/stateless/codec.test.ts is a good deep-dive into the stateless module from Step 6, testing HKDF isolation, tamper detection, and key rotation.

tour.title: Containerization & CI/CD
tour.description: The Dockerfile uses a two-stage Alpine build: the builder stage installs Node.js dev dependencies and compiles TypeScript to ./build, then the runtime stage copies only the compiled output and production dependencies into a minimal Alpine image that starts the server on port 3002. docker/docker-compose.yaml provides a one-command local deployment wiring the container to environment variables. The GitHub Actions workflows complete the picture: pr-test.yml runs four parallel CI jobs (tests, integration, lint, coverage) on every PR; npm-publish.yml publishes to npm on release; docker-publish.yml builds and pushes multi-arch (amd64/arm64) images to Docker Hub.
tour.languageLesson: Multi-stage Docker builds use multiple FROM statements. The builder stage has dev dependencies (TypeScript, type definitions) for compilation, while the final stage copies only the ./build output and production node_modules, keeping the runtime image free of unnecessary build tooling and reducing attack surface.
